section.title: Orderly Worship
section.sectionRationale: Having grounded the gifts in the one Spirit, chapter 12, and crowned them with love, chapter 13, Paul now applies both to the disordered worship at Corinth. Their love of tongues had made their gatherings unintelligible and chaotic. Paul's governing rule is edification: pursue love, seek gifts that build up the church, and let everything be done for the good of all, decently and in order, because God is not a God of disorder but of peace.
section.thesis: In the assembly the church should pursue love and desire above all the gifts that build others up, so prophecy, which is understood, is to be preferred to uninterpreted tongues, and everything is to be done for edification, decently and in order, because God is not a God of disorder but of peace.
section.frameNote: Four movements: prophecy builds up the church more than uninterpreted tongues; intelligible speech is what edifies; tongues and prophecy as signs to unbelievers; and order in the assembly, so that all is done for edification, decently and in order.

units.label: Prophecy builds up more than tongues

verses.text: Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of {{propheteia|prophecy}}.
For he who speaks in a {{glossa|tongue}} does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
But he who prophesies speaks to men for their {{oikodome|edification}}, encouragement, and comfort.
The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church.

I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy. He who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.

units.label: Intelligible speech edifies
units.note: five clear words over ten thousand in a tongue

verses.text: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you, unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
Even in the case of lifeless instruments, such as the flute or harp, how will anyone recognize the tune they are playing unless the notes are distinct?
Again, if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?
So it is with you. Unless you speak intelligible words with your tongue, how will anyone know what you are saying? You will just be speaking into the air.
Assuredly, there are many different languages in the world, yet none of them is without meaning.
If, then, I do not know the meaning of someone’s language, I am a foreigner to the speaker, and he is a foreigner to me.
It is the same with you. Since you are eager to have spiritual gifts, strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.
Therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.
For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.
What then shall I do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind. I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.
Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in spirit, how can someone who is uninstructed say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying?
You may be giving thanks well enough, but the other one is not edified.
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.
But in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.
Brothers, stop thinking like children. In regard to evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.
It is written in the Law: “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord.”
Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers. Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers.
So if the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?
But if an unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in while everyone is prophesying, he will be convicted and called to account by all,
and the secrets of his heart will be made known. So he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, “God is truly among you!”

units.label: Order in the assembly
units.note: God is not a God of disorder but of peace

verses.text: What then shall we say, brothers? When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church.
If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret.
But if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God.
Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said.
And if a revelation comes to someone who is seated, the first speaker should stop.
For you can all prophesy in turn so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged.
The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.
For God is not a God of disorder, but of {{eirene|peace}}, as in all the churches of the saints.
Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says.
If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home; for it is dishonorable for a woman to speak in the church.
Did the word of God originate with you? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command.
But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored.
So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.
But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.

propheteia.gloss: Prophecy, a Spirit-prompted message spoken to people for their edification, encouragement, and comfort. Because it is understood, it builds up the church, convicts outsiders, and instructs all; Paul urges the Corinthians to desire it above uninterpreted tongues, always to be weighed by the others against Scripture.

glossa.gloss: Tongue, meaning both the physical organ and a language. In this chapter it is the gift of speaking in a tongue that no one present understands unless it is interpreted. Paul values it but insists that in the assembly what cannot be understood cannot edify, so tongues need interpretation to serve the church.

oikodome.gloss: Building up, edification, literally the construction of a house. It is the governing rule of the chapter: every gift in the gathering is measured by whether it builds up the church. What edifies the whole body is to be preferred, which is why intelligible prophecy outranks uninterpreted tongues.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, and well-ordered harmony. God is not a God of disorder but of peace, so worship that reflects His character is orderly rather than chaotic. Peace here is not mere quiet but the settled order that lets the whole church be edified and God be honored.

basic.context: The Corinthians loved the gift of tongues and let it dominate their gatherings, even when no one could understand what was said. Paul does not ban tongues, but he insists that the point of coming together is to build up the church, and that only happens through what people can understand. So he urges them to pursue love and to prefer prophecy, which speaks plainly to people. He then gives practical rules so that worship is orderly, because the God they worship is a God of peace, not confusion.
basic.hermeneutics: This is applied instruction for the gathered church, flowing directly from love, chapter 13, and the one body, chapter 12. The controlling principle, edification, must guide how we read the specific rules. Some directions address a particular disorder at Corinth, but the abiding principles are clear: worship should be intelligible, orderly, and aimed at building up everyone, because that reflects God's own character.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul prefers propheteia, prophecy, because it is understood and so edifies, over a glossa, a tongue, that no one can follow without interpretation. The whole chapter is governed by oikodome, building up: every gift in the gathering is measured by whether it edifies the church. And the reason worship must be orderly is that God is a God of eirene, peace, not disorder.
basic.typology: The strange tongues Paul cites from Isaiah were a sign of judgment on an unbelieving Israel who would not listen. Ordered, Spirit-filled worship in which an outsider falls down and confesses God is truly among you fulfills the promise that the nations would come and worship the God of Israel. The gathered church becomes the place where God's presence is made known.
basic.christ: The Spirit's gifts exist to build up the body of Christ and to make Christ known, so that even an unbeliever, convicted by plain prophecy, falls down and worships God. Christ is the head who orders His body, and the peace that must mark the assembly is the peace He secured and gives. Worship that edifies and is orderly displays the character of the Lord who is its center.
basic.god: God is not a God of disorder but of peace, and this truth governs the whole chapter. What we do in worship should reflect who God is. He desires that all be built up, that outsiders be drawn to worship Him, and that His people gather in a way that mirrors His own peace and order rather than chaos and self-display.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 2 records tongues understood by hearers at Pentecost. Romans 12 urges gifts used in proportion to faith for the body. 1 Corinthians 12 grounds this chapter in the one body and one Spirit. 1 Corinthians 11 shows women praying and prophesying in the assembly, bearing on the instruction in verses 34 and 35.
basic.oneStory: God has always gathered a people to worship Him, and He means their worship to draw the nations in. Corinth's chaos obscured His presence; ordered, understandable, loving worship reveals it, so that outsiders confess God is truly among you. This points toward the great assembly of the redeemed from every tongue who will worship God in perfect order and peace around His throne.

context.literary:
Chapter 14 is the third panel of a long argument that began at 12:1. Chapter 12 gave the body and its many members, chapter 13 gave the way of love, and chapter 14 brings both into the room where the church actually meets. Its shape is easy to trace. Verses 1 to 5 state the thesis. Verses 6 to 12 offer three pictures from ordinary life: a flute or harp that plays no distinct tune, a trumpet that sounds a muffled call, and a foreign language that leaves speaker and hearer strangers to each other. Verses 13 to 19 turn to prayer and song and bring Paul himself in as an example. Verses 20 to 25 appeal for grown-up thinking and read the effect of tongues and prophecy on an outsider. Verses 26 to 33 give working rules, and verses 34 to 40 close with a few firm words about authority and a summary.

The chapter is wrapped in an inclusio. It opens with 'Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy,' verse 1, and it closes with 'be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues,' verse 39. Between those two bookends the building language keeps returning, in verses 3, 4, 5, 12, 17 and 26, so that the reader is trained to ask one question of every gift: who is built up by this?

Paul also argues by a repeated pair of postures. Again and again he sets the self against the other, the one who edifies himself against the one who edifies the church, the speaker against the listener. And he writes in the first person, 'I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind,' verse 15, so the correction arrives as shared practice rather than scolding.
context.historical:
Paul is writing from Ephesus, 16:8, to a church meeting in private houses in a busy port city where many languages could be heard in the street. Households such as that of Gaius, whom Romans 16:23 calls host to the whole church, would have supplied the rooms. A gathering there was a crowded, informal affair, and verses 23 and 24 assume that an outsider might simply wander in and find himself in the middle of it.

The Corinthians had come out of a religious world in which inspired, ecstatic speech was prized, and Paul reminds them in 12:2 that they were once led astray to mute idols. It is likely that some prized tongues as a mark of spiritual rank, which would explain why Paul keeps tying the gifts back to the good of others, and why he says in verse 18 that he himself speaks in tongues more than all of them, so that no one can suppose he despises the gift out of ignorance.

Prophecy in the New Testament church was real speech from God, but it was subject to testing. Israel already had its rules for judging prophets, Deuteronomy 18:20 to 22, and the early church kept them, which is why verse 29 tells the others to weigh what is said, and 1 Thessalonians 5:19 to 21 says to test everything. The women Paul mentions in verses 34 and 35 are the same ones he assumed would pray and prophesy aloud in 11:5, so the instruction has to be read as part of an ordered meeting where a disruption was happening, and not as a general muting of half the congregation.
context.canonical:
The chapter is full of Old Testament echoes. Its wish, 'I would rather have you prophesy,' verse 5, recalls Moses, who answered a jealous complaint with, 'I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!' Numbers 11:29. Joel had promised that very outpouring, Joel 2:28 to 29, and Peter said at Pentecost that it had come, Acts 2:16 to 18. The sign of foreign tongues in verse 21 comes from Isaiah 28:11 to 12, where the strange speech of the Assyrian invader was a warning to a people who had refused plain prophetic words, and behind that lies Deuteronomy 28:49, the threat of a nation whose language Israel would not understand.

Pentecost itself is the model of intelligible tongues: 'each one heard them speaking in his own language,' Acts 2:6. It stands as the answer to Babel, Genesis 11:7 to 9, where speech was scrambled so that people could no longer understand one another. Elsewhere the gift appears at Cornelius's house, Acts 10:44 to 46, and at Ephesus, Acts 19:6, always as a sign that the Spirit had been given.

The New Testament carries the central principle further. Ephesians 4:11 to 16 says the gifts exist to equip the saints until the body builds itself up in love. 1 Peter 4:10 to 11 tells each one to use whatever gift he has to serve others. And the picture in verse 25, of a stranger who 'will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, "God is truly among you!"' echoes Isaiah 45:14, where the nations come to Israel saying that God is with them. The book of Revelation finally gathers people from every tongue before the throne, Revelation 7:9, so that the diversity of languages is not erased but redeemed.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted a church that was proud of its gifts to become a church that was eager for its neighbour's good. He was not trying to put out the fire of the Spirit. He says plainly that he wishes they all spoke in tongues, verse 5, and he forbids anyone to forbid it, verse 39. What he wanted changed was the measuring stick. The Corinthians had been asking, 'What does this show about me?' Paul teaches them to ask, 'Who is helped by this?'

He also meant them to grow up. 'Stop thinking like children,' verse 20, is addressed to people who were rather pleased with their spiritual impressiveness. Mature faith, he says, is not less spiritual but more thoughtful: it prays with the mind as well as the spirit, sings with both, and wants the stranger in the room to understand.

And he intended the church to recognise the character of God in its own gatherings. The rule for order is not rooted in a love of tidiness but in the nature of God, verse 33, so that a meeting which is calm, clear and kind says something true about the One who is being worshipped. The first hearers were meant to leave with a simple practice: speak in turn, make it plain, test what is said, and let love be the measure.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this chapter is a direct command, and it still binds: build one another up, make speech intelligible, speak in turn, interpret what is said in tongues or keep silent, weigh prophecy, and do all things properly and in order, verses 26 to 40. Those are rules for the gathered church, and they apply wherever a church gathers.

Some details, however, describe the shape of the Corinthian problem rather than lay down a pattern for every congregation. The limit of two or three speakers, verse 27, belongs to a meeting where everyone brought something, verse 26, and its purpose is that no one dominates and all are heard. A church with a different order of service keeps the purpose and may adapt the number. Likewise the examples of musical instruments and foreign languages are illustrations, not regulations.

Care is needed with verses 34 and 35. They describe a restriction Paul gives in the setting of weighing prophecy, and they must be read alongside 11:5, where women pray and prophesy in the assembly. Churches differ in how widely they apply the instruction, and the fair approach is to hold the text together with its neighbours rather than to lift it out alone. What nobody may do is turn the chapter into an excuse for a lifeless, silent worship. Paul's closing words, 'be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues,' keep the door of the Spirit open even as the order is kept.

debates.question: What does Paul mean that women are to be silent in the churches, verses 34 and 35?

views.label: A specific restriction within the flow of order
views.case: Since 11:5 assumes women praying and prophesying in the assembly, many read the silence as directed at a particular disruption, such as the disorderly weighing or questioning of prophecies, so women were not to interrupt the judging of prophecy but to ask at home, keeping the same order Paul urges of tongues-speakers and prophets. The same Greek verb for being silent was just used of the tongues-speaker without an interpreter, verse 28, and of the prophet who yields, verse 30, so silence here is the silence of a particular situation.

views.label: A broader ordering of the assembly's authoritative speech
views.case: Others take it as a wider instruction, consistent with 1 Timothy 2:11 to 12, that in the gathered church the authoritative teaching and public judging of prophecy is not for women to lead, while still allowing the praying and prophesying of 11:5, so submission as the law says orders the assembly rather than silencing every voice.

debates.bearing: Both orthodox readings honor the whole of Scripture, hold together with 11:5, and aim at peace and order in worship rather than the silencing or devaluing of women; the difference is over the scope of the restriction. It is also worth noting the textual point that some manuscripts place verses 34 and 35 after verse 40, though the verses are present in the tradition and are handled here as part of the text.

debates.question: What is the gift of tongues in this chapter?

views.label: Real human languages
views.case: The comparison with the many languages of the world, verses 10 and 11, and the pattern of Acts 2 suggest actual languages unknown to the speaker, which is why an interpreter is needed for the church to understand.

views.label: Spirit-prompted utterance needing interpretation
views.case: That the speaker addresses God and utters mysteries no one understands, verse 2, and that his mind is unfruitful, verse 14, suggests a Spirit-given prayer language that must be interpreted to edify others.

debates.bearing: On either view Paul's point holds: a tongue that no one present understands cannot build up the church unless it is interpreted, so in the assembly intelligible prophecy is to be preferred.

debates.question: How can tongues be a sign for unbelievers in verse 22 when verse 23 says they drive unbelievers away?

views.label: A sign of judgment, not of blessing
views.case: Paul has just quoted Isaiah, where strange tongues were the sign that God was speaking to a people who would not listen. Read that way, tongues without interpretation confirm unbelievers in their unbelief, and the outsider simply concludes the church is mad, verse 23. Prophecy, by contrast, reaches into the heart, verses 24 and 25.

views.label: A sign that needs interpretation to become a sign of grace
views.case: Others hold that the sign is neutral until it is understood: tongues attract attention, as at Pentecost, but only when they are made intelligible do they lead to repentance. Verses 22 and 23 then simply say that a sign nobody can read is no sign at all.

debates.bearing: Either way Paul's practical conclusion is the same: in the assembly, plain speech that exposes the heart and calls people to worship is to be preferred to speech that bewilders an outsider.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul urges them to 'eagerly desire' spiritual gifts, verse 1, and later to be 'eager' to prophesy, verse 39, and he says they are 'eager to have spiritual gifts,' verse 12. The verb behind each is zeloo, to be zealous or to burn with desire, and it frames the whole chapter. His point is not to dampen zeal but to aim it. The word he uses for 'spiritual gifts' in verse 1 is simply the neuter plural pneumatika, 'spiritual things,' the same term that opened the whole discussion at 12:1. Paul's first command is dioko, to pursue, a hunting word, so that love is something to be chased down and not merely admired.

In verse 14 Paul contrasts 'my spirit' with 'my mind,' the Greek nous. When he prays in a tongue his spirit prays but his nous is unfruitful. In verse 15 he refuses to choose between them, 'I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind,' and in verse 19 he would rather speak five words 'with my mind' than ten thousand in a tongue. The Greek nous is the faculty that grasps and understands, so Paul is refusing to treat spirituality as a sphere beyond thought.

The outsider of verses 16, 23 and 24 is called an idiotes, translated 'uninstructed.' The word originally meant a private person, one without a particular expertise, and here it names someone who is not yet part of the circle that understands what is going on. In verse 16 he cannot say the 'Amen' because he cannot follow, which shows that the Amen is a shared, thoughtful assent and not a reflex.

Verse 29 says the others should 'weigh carefully' what is said. The verb is diakrino, to distinguish or discern, the same root that turns up in 12:10 for the 'distinguishing between spirits.' Prophecy is received, but it is received critically.

Three verbs in a row share a family. In verses 28, 30 and 34 the verb siga, to be silent, is used of the tongues-speaker with no interpreter, of the first prophet when a revelation comes to another, and of women. Verse 32 and verse 34 share the verb hypotasso, 'to be subject.' The spirits of prophets are 'subject' to prophets, so inspiration does not overpower self-control; and then the same verb describes the submission required in verse 34. A reader who wants to understand either verse has to hold the family together.

The closing command, verse 40, asks that all things be done euschemonos, 'decently' or becomingly, and kata taxin, 'according to order.' Taxis is an orderly arrangement, and the same word is used elsewhere of ranks in an army or the arrangement of a household. Verse 33 chooses the opposite, akatastasia, literally a state of not-standing-together, 'disorder' or unrest. The contrast of taxis and akatastasia is the contrast between a meeting that stands together and one that comes apart. Finally, in verse 20 Paul says 'stop thinking like children' and to be 'mature,' teleioi. In 2:6 he used the same word of those who grasp the wisdom of God.

typology.type: Babel, Pentecost and the intelligible assembly
typology.fulfillment: At Babel God scrambled human speech so that people could no longer understand one another, Genesis 11:7 to 9. At Pentecost the reverse was heard: 'each one heard them speaking in his own language,' Acts 2:6, and the nations were gathered into one hearing of the mighty works of God. Paul's insistence on interpretation in the assembly continues that line, since a gathering where no one understands is Babel in miniature, and one in which all understand is a foretaste of Pentecost. The escalation comes at the end, when people from every tongue stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The type falls short because Pentecost's languages were a sign, while the final gathering will be a settled fact.

typology.type: Foreign tongues as a sign of judgment
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 28:11 to 12 warned a people who had mocked the prophet's plain words that God would speak to them in the strange language of an invader, and Deuteronomy 28:49 had named that threat long before. The Assyrian speech was a sign, a loud one, that God was not being heard. In Corinth the same pattern is possible in miniature: when the church speaks only in unintelligible words, an outsider hears a sign of distance and not of welcome. The correspondence reaches its climax in the Word who became flesh, John 1:14, and so made God's speech finally understandable. The type falls short in that Israel's sign was judgment, while the church's gifts are given for blessing.

typology.type: The sanctuary where God is among His people
typology.fulfillment: God told Israel to build the tabernacle 'according to the pattern,' Exodus 25:9, and promised, 'I will dwell among the Israelites,' Exodus 29:45. Paul calls the church God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and in 14:25 the outsider's confession, 'God is truly among you,' is the verdict the tabernacle was built to produce. Orderly worship is the new sanctuary order. The escalation is that the dwelling is no longer a tent of cloth and gold but a people indwelt by the Spirit, Ephesians 2:21 to 22. The type falls short in that the tabernacle was a place a few priests could enter, whereas the new temple is open to all who believe.

typology.type: Moses' wish that all would prophesy
typology.fulfillment: When Joshua wanted to stop two men prophesying in the camp, Moses answered, 'I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets,' Numbers 11:29. That wish was a hope for a day when the Spirit would be on every member of God's people, and Joel gave it a promise, Joel 2:28 to 29. Paul's words, 'you can all prophesy in turn,' verse 31, show the hope arriving, since the prophetic Spirit now rests on the whole church. The type falls short in that Moses wished it only for Israel, and the new covenant gives it to every nation.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the Spirit who gives the gifts. Paul has already said that the Spirit gives them 'for the common good,' 12:7, and he has already said that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says 'Jesus be cursed,' 12:3. The test of a gift is therefore christological: does it make Christ known and build His body? This is why the outsider in verse 25 does not leave admiring a speaker but confesses 'God is truly among you.' Prophecy is meant to bring the stranger to the feet of the One it is about.

It leads to Christ as head of the body. The body of Christ is not a loose crowd but an ordered organism, and Ephesians 4:15 to 16 says that the whole body, joined and held together by every supporting ligament, grows by speaking the truth in love. The instruction in 14:26 that 'all of these must be done to build up the church' is the working out of that growth. The assembly is a place where the risen Lord is present, Matthew 18:20, and the gifts are His means of speaking to His people.

It leads to Christ by contrast with the confusion that Paul fears. The Lord who stilled a storm with a word, Mark 4:39, is the author of peace, and Paul will not let His church imitate the noise it was rescued from. The peace of verse 33 is not mere calm; it is the peace Christ made by the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20, and gives to His people, John 14:27. A church that meets in His peace carries His mark.

It leads to Christ by the way of love. The chapter's first command, 'Earnestly pursue love,' follows directly from 13:1 to 13, and the pattern of that love is Christ Himself, who did not please Himself, Romans 15:3, and who 'did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. When Paul sets a person's own display aside for another's benefit, he is asking the Corinthians to copy the pattern of the Son. Paul says elsewhere, 'Each of us should please his neighbor for his good, to build him up,' Romans 15:2, and the next verse points to Christ as the example.

It leads to Christ by His speech. In the Gospels Jesus spoke so that people could understand, and He often used pictures from ordinary life, as Paul does with the flute and the trumpet. He told His disciples to listen carefully to what they heard, Mark 4:24. In verse 36 Paul asks, 'Did the word of God originate with you?' and the answer is that the word came through Christ, Hebrews 1:1 to 2. The church receives, and does not own, the word it speaks.

A caution is needed. The chapter is not a hidden portrait of Christ in every detail. The flute, the trumpet and the five coherent words are Paul's illustrations, and they are not types. The links to Christ run through the Spirit, the body and the love that the chapter names openly, and they are strong enough that nothing needs forcing.
study.god:
The chapter's great statement about God is in verse 33: 'God is not a God of disorder, but of peace.' It is not an argument from taste. God has revealed Himself as a God who orders. Genesis 1 shows Him bringing form out of what was formless and void, and the sequence of creation days is a pattern of order. The sanctuary was built to a pattern, and even Israel's camp was arranged by tribe, Numbers 2. Paul draws the conclusion for worship: the way we gather ought to resemble the One we gather before.

He is the God of peace, the Greek eirene, which in the Bible means more than the absence of noise. It means wholeness and right relation. Paul uses this title often, as in Romans 15:33, 'the God of peace be with you all,' and 2 Corinthians 13:11. A church that makes peace in its assembly is a witness to who He is.

He is the God who speaks to be understood. The whole chapter assumes that God wants His words received by minds as well as hearts. He does not dwell on mystery for its own sake; in Scripture He reveals, instructs and calls to account, and His prophets were sent with a message the people could grasp. Paul's own wish, to speak five words with his mind, reflects a God who addresses real people in real language.

He is the God who knows hearts. The outsider in verse 25 finds that 'the secrets of his heart will be made known,' and the result is not shame alone but worship. Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart, and in the chapter that judgment is a mercy, because it ends with a man on his face confessing God.

He is the generous giver. Every gift in the chapter, the psalm, the teaching, the revelation, the tongue and the interpretation, comes from Him, and Paul has already said the Spirit distributes them as He determines, 12:11. Nothing in the chapter treats the gifts as dangerous or unwelcome. It treats them as gifts to be held with open hands for others' good.

He is the God who is truly present. The outsider's cry, 'God is truly among you,' is the very thing the tabernacle and temple were built to testify. God does not simply receive worship; He is in the midst of it, and the gathered church is the place where His presence is found.

Tension is held here in a healthy way. God gives gifts that are beyond human understanding, such as tongues, and yet He asks that they be ordered and interpreted. He is free and He is orderly; He is Spirit and He is peace. For worship this means that we may expect His presence and still keep the doors of the meeting open to the stranger, and that the best worship is the kind in which He is both honoured and understood.

crossReferences.note: The first and clearest picture of tongues in the New Testament, where Galileans spoke and visitors from many lands heard 'the wonders of God' each in his own language. It shows what Paul wants at Corinth: Spirit-given speech that the hearers can understand. Where Pentecost reversed Babel, Corinth risked repeating it.

'Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.' This sentence is the root of the whole chapter. Chapter 14 is simply the working out of 'common good' in the meeting, so that every gift, however impressive, is judged by whom it helps and not by how it looks.

Paul had already assumed that women pray and prophesy in the church's gathering. Any reading of 14:34 and 35 has to keep this earlier statement in view, so that the later verses are understood as an instruction about a particular order or disruption, not a flat denial of what chapter 11 permits.

The text Paul calls 'the Law' in verse 21. Isaiah told scornful leaders that God would speak to them through the strange speech of foreign invaders, and 'even then they will not listen.' Paul uses it to show that unintelligible speech can be a sign of distance and judgment, and not of welcome.

A parallel text on women and teaching, written to Timothy in Ephesus. Readers who see 1 Corinthians 14:34 and 35 as a wider restriction connect the two, and those who read it as local connect it with the setting of each letter. Either way the two passages are best read together.

Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets is the background for verse 5 and verse 31. Paul rejoices that the prophetic Spirit is now given widely, and he arranges the meeting so that this widely given gift serves all.

'Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good.' This is the same balance as verse 29 and verse 39: welcome the gift and weigh what is said, neither silencing the Spirit nor swallowing every message unexamined.

Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists and pastors and teachers to equip the saints so that the body builds itself up in love. It supplies the purpose behind Paul's building language in 14:3 to 5 and 26, and shows that edification is not a church-meeting rule but the way Christ grows His body.

The Spirit intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words, and God knows the mind of the Spirit. It helps explain why Paul can say that a person praying in a tongue speaks to God and not to men, verse 2, without despising the mind that is also given to us.

'Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.' The same contrast shapes chapter 14: the Corinthians' pride in knowledge and in gifts had to be corrected by the love that builds. Paul uses the same verb for edifying in both places, which shows how steadily he returns to it.

study.oneStory:
The question of this chapter is as old as Babel: how can a scattered, many-tongued humanity become one people who understand each other and worship together? In Genesis 11 the nations were divided by language and sent out across the earth. The rest of the Bible tells how God gathers them again. Abraham was told that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and Israel's prophets pictured the nations streaming to Zion to learn God's ways, Isaiah 2:2 to 3.

Israel was meant to be the place where that gathering began, a people among whom God dwelt, Exodus 29:45. But Israel often turned the sanctuary into a place of noise and show, and the prophets rebuked worship that was loud and loveless, Amos 5:21 to 24. Isaiah 28 shows the sad end of that path: a people who would not hear God plainly are given strange speech as a sign.

Pentecost begins the reversal. The Spirit is poured out, and the gospel is heard in the languages of the nations, Acts 2:5 to 11. The church becomes the new temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16, in which Jew and Gentile are joined, Ephesians 2:19 to 22. Corinth is an early test case of whether that new gathering will look like heaven or like Babel. Paul's answer is that it will look like heaven when love directs the gifts, when speech is understood, and when strangers are welcomed and moved to worship.

The chapter points ahead as well. Every gift here belongs to the present age; Paul has just said that tongues and prophecy will cease while love remains, 13:8 to 10. What is practised in this broken age is practised in partial knowledge, 13:12, and it points to a day of full knowledge. The church of the future will not need an interpreter, for 'a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, tribe, people, and language' will stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9.

The new creation is the final answer to the problem of 1 Corinthians 14. Babel's confusion is undone, the people of God worship in perfect understanding, and God's presence is no longer 'truly among' them in the way a stranger discovers it, but fully with them, Revelation 21:3. The order that Paul asks for now is a rehearsal for that peace.

quiz.q: Why does Paul prefer prophecy to uninterpreted tongues in the assembly?

options.text: Because prophecy is understood and so builds up the whole church, while an uninterpreted tongue does not.
options.note: Verses 3 to 5: prophecy edifies the church; a tongue needs interpretation.

options.text: Because tongues are a false gift that should be banned.
options.note: Paul does not forbid tongues; he ranks understandable speech higher for the gathering.

options.text: Because only prophecy comes from the Holy Spirit.
options.note: Both are Spirit-given; the issue is intelligibility and edification.

options.text: Because prophecy is more impressive to onlookers.
options.note: The point is edification and clarity, not spectacle.

quiz.q: What single principle governs how gifts are used when the church gathers?

options.text: Everything must be done to build up the church.
options.note: Verse 26: all of these must be done to build up the church.

options.text: Everyone should use their most dramatic gift freely.
options.note: Free self-expression is exactly what Paul reins in for the sake of edification.

options.text: Only the leaders should exercise any gift.
options.note: Many may contribute; the rule is that it must edify, in order.

options.text: Whatever feels most spiritual in the moment.
options.note: The measure is edification, not private feeling.

quiz.q: How does Paul say an unbeliever may respond to clear prophecy?

options.text: He is convicted, the secrets of his heart exposed, and falls down to worship, saying God is truly among you.
options.note: Verses 24 and 25 describe conviction and worship.

options.text: He is impressed by the display of tongues.
options.note: Verse 23 says tongues alone may make outsiders think you are mad.

options.text: He is left unaffected either way.
options.note: Prophecy convicts and calls him to account; he is deeply affected.

options.text: He is driven away by the strictness of the rules.
options.note: He is drawn to worship, confessing God's presence.

quiz.q: What reason does Paul give for orderly worship?

options.text: God is not a God of disorder but of peace.
options.note: Verse 33 grounds order in the character of God.

options.text: Because disorder is illegal in the city of Corinth.
options.note: The reason is theological, rooted in who God is, not civil law.

options.text: Because the leaders prefer quiet meetings.
options.note: It is grounded in God's character, not leaders' preference.

options.text: Because spiritual gifts are dangerous and should be limited.
options.note: Paul affirms the gifts; order reflects God's peace, not fear of gifts.

quiz.q: How should verses 34 and 35 on women being silent be read responsibly?

options.text: In light of the whole passage and of 11:5, as ordering the assembly for peace, with orthodox interpreters differing on its exact scope.
options.note: It must be held together with 11:5, where women pray and prophesy, and read under the theme of order.

options.text: As a total ban on women ever speaking or ministering at all.
options.note: That collides with 11:5 and the wider New Testament; the scope is debated among the orthodox.

options.text: As an outdated rule with nothing to teach the church.
options.note: It is part of inspired Scripture and addresses order in worship, not to be dismissed.

options.text: As proof that the passage is not really Paul's teaching.
options.note: The verses are in the text; a manuscript note on their placement does not overturn their authority.

questions: Paul measures everything in the gathering by whether it builds others up. When you come to church, are you thinking mainly about your own experience or about edifying the people around you?
He would rather speak five words people understand than ten thousand they cannot. Where might clarity and love for others matter more than impressive-sounding spirituality in your own service?
Prophecy laid bare the secrets of an outsider's heart until he worshiped. How does it change your view of gathered worship to see it as a place where God draws in those who do not yet believe?
God is a God of peace, not disorder, and our worship should reflect His character. What would it look like for your church's gatherings to display God's peace more fully?

This chapter asks us to weigh contested instructions carefully and humbly alongside the rest of Scripture. How can you hold firm convictions on debated matters while still honoring fellow believers who read them differently?

translationNotes.note: Edification translates oikodome, literally the building of a house; it is the governing measure of the chapter, so every gift in the gathering is weighed by whether it builds up the church.

That tongues are a sign for unbelievers draws on Isaiah 28, where foreign tongues signaled judgment on an unbelieving people; the point is not that tongues evangelize but that unintelligible speech leaves outsiders in the dark.

This instruction must be read alongside 11:5, where women pray and prophesy in the assembly; orthodox interpreters differ on its exact scope. Some manuscripts place verses 34 and 35 after verse 40, though the verses are attested in the manuscript tradition.
